solution:
**(C)** sarcomere

The sarcomere, the stretch of a myofibril between two Z-lines, is the contractile unit of striated muscle: its actin and myosin filaments slide past each other to shorten it. A myofibril is a chain of many sarcomeres, the Z-band is only the boundary of a sarcomere, and the cross bridges are the myosin heads that act within it.

**(B)** Tarsal

The seven tarsals are the bones of the ankle; the talus among them articulates with the tibia. Metatarsals form the sole of the foot, while carpals and metacarpals are the wrist and palm bones of the hand.

**(B)** lactic acid

During strenuous exercise the oxygen supply falls short, so muscles respire anaerobically and pyruvic acid is reduced to lactic acid. Lactic acid accumulates and causes tiredness, pain and cramps, which is muscle fatigue. Pyruvic, malic and succinic acids are intermediates that are used up in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle rather than accumulating.

**(D)** Sphinetro-suprinater

This misprinted option pairs a sphincter with a supinator. Antagonistic muscles produce opposite actions at the same part: flexor and extensor, adductor and abductor, levator and depressor. A sphincter is a circular muscle that closes an opening such as the anus, while the supinator turns the palm upward; its true antagonist is the pronator.

**(A)** due to osmosis

Strong salt water is hypertonic to the tissue fluid, so water moves out of the swollen tissue into the salt solution through the skin, and the swelling goes down. Plasmolysis is the shrinking of a plant cell's protoplast away from its cell wall, and electrolysis and photolysis are splitting by electricity and by light.

[Note: the chapter does not state this; standard biology gives osmotic withdrawal of water into a hypertonic solution.]

**(B)** to bind with troponin, changing its shape so that the actin filament is exposed

When an impulse arrives, calcium ions are released into the sarcoplasm and bind troponin. This changes the troponin-tropomyosin complex so that tropomyosin moves off the active sites of actin, and myosin heads can attach and pull. Breaking cross bridges needs fresh ATP, the impulse crosses the neuromuscular junction by acetylcholine, and repolarisation is the work of the ion pumps, not calcium.

**(C)** Osteoporosis

Parathormone raises blood calcium by drawing calcium out of bone. Too much of it makes bone resorption outpace bone formation, so the bones lose mass and become porous and brittle, which is osteoporosis. Gout comes from uric acid deposits, rheumatoid arthritis is autoimmune, and Gull's disease is myxoedema from too little thyroid hormone.

[Note: the chapter does not state this; standard biology gives bone demineralisation as the effect of excess parathormone.]

**(C)** Drawing: two bars with square ends meeting along a straight vertical line

The two nasal bones meet in a butt joint, a suture whose bones have square edges that simply abut. The tapering, slanting joint is a scarf joint, the overlapping one is a lap joint (as between temporal and parietal bones), and the zig-zag interlocking one is a serrate joint found between various skull bones.
